Github's Revamped Pull Request Experience

How might we improve the code review process for better collaboration among developers?

Impact:

50M+

Active Users

1.5M+

Daily Pull Requests

Potentially streamlining workflow for millions of developers globally

In early 2024, GitHub launched a redesigned code review experience in beta  aimed at improving accessibility. Our team was tasked with testing this change, and improving it before its wider release. What we discovered went far beyond usability metrics – it revealed how developers actually collaborate around code.

This work influenced a core feature used by over 100M developers, impacting how GitHub thinks about accessibility, collaboration and workflow design.

What difference did we make?

Understanding Code Review

Every piece of software you use was shaped by thousands of conversations between developers. These conversations happen through code reviews.

Think of code review like editing a document, but instead of suggesting grammar changes, developers are discussing how to make software work better.

A Pull request, made by code author, invites code reviewers to provide feedback and approve changes before merging

What prompted us to look deeper?

The Accessibility Paradox

From 2020 to 2023, GitHub had been working to make their platform more accessible. But something unexpected happened during testing:

the new "accessible" design scored lower (66.75) than the original UI (75.5) in usability tests.

If this went to production, it would impact millions of daily developer conversations.

66.75

New UI SUS Score

<

75.5

Original UI SUS Score

Our problem was to evaluate, test and suggest fixes to this new design.

What was the new "accessible" design?

The new design introduced "floating comments" - a major shift from traditional inline comments.

The idea was simple:

Keep code views cleaner

Make comments less intrusive

Allow simultaneous code and comment viewing

The new floating comments seemed cleaner in theory, but in reality users had several problems with it.

Building understanding through Research

To understand what was really happening, we needed to build a complete picture of how developers actually work. We performed a whole range of detailed quantitative & qualitative studies with 6+ experienced software developers to inform our design decisions

Scenarios & Tasks

To account for the two UIs (old and new) and two user roles (Code Author and Code Reviewer), we created four testing environments, each participant was subjected to sections with varying orders of the testing environments.

The varied order of exposure to the UIs, as shown above, helped mitigate potential biases, such as increased preference for the first interface encountered.

Understanding the Current State

GitHub's code review process has evolved over the years, growing to serve diverse needs and workflows.

Our research revealed key realities of how developers actually work:

Multiple monitor setups dominate

Comments vary from quick fixes to long discussions

Teams collaborate across time zones asynchronously

Accessibility needs vary widely

Making sense of large amount of qualitative data

What was missing?

Connection

Developers lost the thread of conversations across files and needed help finding discussions across files.

Context

Hidden comments made developers lose their train of thought. Each expansion broke focus.

Control

Accessibility features like floating comments actually reduced control for many users

How did this make the developers feel?

Overwhelmed & missing the original interface

Findings & Solutions

Making it Right

Comments are inefficient for Multi-monitor setups

What we found

“

I have to move my mouse quite a lot further for a comment, because generally I'm reading on the left side. Code is never right justified.

4 out of 6 developers use multiple monitors

Right-aligned comments caused constant screen scanning

Breaking this down:

Issue

Mouse travel distance

Fact

Reading happens left-to-right

User Need

Comments should be accessible where attention already is

Various design iterations of how the icon can be made to appear more clearly

Solution: Bring comments to you

Design Recommendation

Make the entire code line interactive: zero additional mouse movement

Moved indicators to the left

Maintained natural code reading flow

Impact

60% reduction in mouse movement

25% faster review completion

Improved focus retention

Users need choice

What we found

“

Having to expand and collapse the comments is tedious, especially if there are many comments I need to check or revisit

Long discussions break flow when floating

Constant expand/collapse fatigue

One-size-fits-all approach failing

Users should be able to toggle between floating & inline comments

Design Recommendation

Moved options to switch between different comment viewing options within the settings

Impact

Better handling of long discussions

Maintained context during review

Improved review flow

Icons are hard to spot

What we found

“

"Depending on the display picture of the user, it might just blend in- like the green logo on the green line would be hard for people to distinguish"

Color-blind users particularly struggled with the new comment indicators on highlighted code.

Easy to miss important comments

Design Recommendation

Enhanced contrast ratios

Clear visual distinction for indicators

Screen reader optimizations

Impact

Improved visibility for all users

Reduced cognitive load

True universal accessibility

Comments are lost in Code forest

What we found

“

I have to scroll a lot to see which file has comments, especially when there's a lot of files

  • P3

No visibility of comment distribution across files

Manual hunting for discussions

Context switching breaking focus

View resulting design Explorations

Tried some variations of comment indicators next to file navigation

Design Recommendations

Added comment counts to file tree

Visual indicators for unresolved discussions

Quick jump to conversation points

Impact

40% faster file navigation

Complete context at a glance

Reduced missed comments

Impact & Learnings

Context is everything

Understanding physical workspaces revealed insights we'd have missed in traditional usability testing. Multiple monitors weren't just a preference – they were fundamental to how developers work.

"Accessible" Isn't Always Accessible

Making something "more accessible" requires understanding all users' actual workflows, not just following guidelines. Sometimes well-intentioned changes can create new barriers.

Small changes have big impact

I discovered the importance of digging deeper into the users’ context of use, as these can reveal interesting insights.

When you're designing for millions of developers, even tiny interactions matter:

3 seconds saved per comment

40% faster file navigation

60% reduction in mouse movement

Our study directly influenced GitHub's development roadmap, prioritizing user experience in this critical feature update.Our design recommendations had great impact, but all software is an infinite experiment. Our findings continue to influence how GitHub approaches accessibility and workflow design, ensuring that future changes enhance rather than hinder the developer experience.

Keeping AI Models in check at HPE

,

Impact:

Overview

Challenge

Solution

Design Process

Key Learnings

Reflections

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) is an enterprise software company providing cutting-edge cloud solutions using AI/ML, analytics for over 10+ industries with 250,000 + customers worldwide.

During my role as a Product Designer at Hewlett Packard Enterprise's Advanced Development Centre, I led the development of an AI model monitoring dashboard. This tool was designed to help data scientists and ML engineers more easily detect and respond to changes in their models' performance over time.

PROBLEM SPACE AND GOAL

The Challenge

AI models can become less accurate over time as they process new data. This problem is called data drift. It makes it hard to keep AI systems working well. Our team at HPE saw that we needed a better way to watch for and fix this issue.

"We're spending more time troubleshooting models because there's just too many different applications to check"

– Data Scientist, HPE

FINAL RESULT

The Solution: AI Monitoring Dashboard

My team and I developed a dashboard that consolidated multiple data streams and analysis tools into a single, intuitive interface. It allowed data scientists across teams to:

Monitor model performance & data distributions in real time

Detect potential issues early

Automate model retraining processes

Collaborate more effectively on model maintenance

DESIGN PROCESS

How we solved it

Talked to Users, then Walked their Shoes:

Interviewed data scientists and ML engineers to understand their current workflows and pain points

Analyzed existing tools and identified areas for improvement

Shadowed users to gain firsthand experience of their challenges

“

"Lot of time & energy spent each week pulling data from different systems just to see how our models are performing. It's tedious and error-prone"

– Senior Data Scientist, HPE

“

"By the time we notice a significant performance drop, it's often too late, and we're scrambling to retrain and redeploy"

– Staff Machine Learning Engineer, HPE

Designing, testing, iterating & more iterating

Created wireframes and user flows focused on simplifying complex data visualization

Developed interactive prototypes with dummy data and iterated based on user feedback

Bringing the Dashboard to Life

Built the dashboard using React and Grommet with the developer, adhering to HPE's design system

Integrated statistical methods for drift detection and performance monitoring

Collaborated closely with data scientists every step of the way to ensure the tool met their needs

Testing in the Wild

Conducted usability testing with real-time, production data to check if it could handle volumes

Iteratively improved the dashboard based on feedback and usage data

Implemented A/B testing for key features to optimize user experience

DESIGN PROCESS

Key Learnings

Complex data mustn’t be dumbed-down for usability

I learned to present complex statistical information in an accessible way without oversimplifying the underlying data. It's a delicate balance between clarity and depth.

Specialized tools need specialised end-user involvement

Through multiple iterations, I discovered the critical importance of involving end-users throughout the design and development process, especially for specialized tools like this dashboard.

Best way to understand the system you’re solving for is to experience it first-hand

Worked closely with data scientists, and shadowing their daily workflow, hugely helped improved both the functionality of the tool and my understanding of ML workflows.

Consider scalability from the start

At a company as large as HPE, I had to design the system to handle monitoring of multiple models efficiently. This presented interesting technical challenges and pushed me to think big from the start.

DESIGN PROCESS

Reflections

Design is indeed a lot of work, but it is fulfilling. This project was my first gig as a designer in big tech right after transitioning from software engineering. As a developer, I'd always underestimated design work - boy, was I wrong. I found myself loving the challenge and creativity of design and really is the origin story of how I decided to be a Designer.

While I can't dive into the specifics due to NDAs, I'm always happy to chat about how this project shaped my approach to designing for complex technical workflows.

Next Up

Sensitizing Invasive Medical Exams

How might we create a safe space for sexual assault survivors during preventative healthcare appointments?

Trigger Warning: Following content contains topics of sexual assault

Impact:

50M+

Active Users

1.5M+

Daily Pull Requests

Impact:

Overview

Challenge

Solution

Design Process

Key Learnings

Reflections

A Safe Space aims to empower patients with a history of trauma and improve patient-provider communication by transforming the physical patient room with smart technology and optimizing the patient booking experience through a redesign of the MyChart booking system.

This initiative addresses a critical gap in trauma-informed healthcare, developed by a team of four from the University of Washington committed to creating meaningful change in patient experiences.

PROBLEM SPACE

The Challenge

Visits to the gynecologist's office often feel cold and transactional. For survivors of sexual trauma, these environments can nurture painful memories when warmth and safety are needed most.

Routine invasive procedures like pelvic exams or pap smears can be retriggering or even retraumatizing.

This project is an attempt to reshape a broken system into one that nurtures healing instead of trauma.

“

"I dread every visit, I feel completely helpless and retriggered. It's terrifying."

– Survivor/Victim about pelvic-exam

FINAL RESULT

Solution Overview

Skip to Final Design >>

RESEARCH

How we arrived at the solution

Sneak Peek into the final design plan

Online Netnography

I scoured existing resources & communities via various reddit threads and forums like nurse.com to learn about survivors' pelvic exam experiences and trauma-informed care through healthcare professionals and patients.

“

One of the hallmarks of trauma experiences is loss of control.

– Survivor

“

I feel helpless when system-related factors hinder their ability to best care for my patients and myself

  • Nurse

On-site Observation

We took a closer look at the patient room by booking an appointment and visiting the space to understand the atmosphere and how it could be made more comforting

Hand-drawn drawings were helpful in making the environment feel warm & safe. Patients rights are displayed at the back of the door.

User Surveys & Interviews

Aiming for a comprehensive rounded view, we reached out far & wide to survivors, healthcare professionals, educators & organizations to collect their insights and experiences by sending out surveys.

Following the survey, interested participants engaged with us in detailed interviews to provide richer, qualitative insights into their experiences.I conducted a 2 out of a total of 6 interviews comprising of Survivors/Victims & Healthcare providers.

“

She sat on a stool where she was not hovering over me, but below me, very reassuring

– Survivor about pelvic exam

“

I was just not prepared to get a pap smear that day, was caught offguard and powerless

– Survivor about pelvic exam

“

It is frustrating to defend my need for care, a basic right

– Survivor/Victim about pelvic-exam

DESIGN PROCESS

Key Findings

User Groups

After thorough analysis of our research data through affinity mapping, we identified crucial patterns and themes. Our research revealed two primary user groups: Survivors/Victims and Healthcare Providers

Advocate Survivors

Empowered individuals asserting their needs

“It’s not my job to explain my survivorship”

Hesitant Survivors

Those struggling with trust in medical settings

“I have a really difficult time feeling comfortable with doctors”

Seasoned Practitioner

Experienced practitioners with limited time

“I don’t have enough time to talk through the exam process for each patient”

Eager Residents

Eager residents aiming to provide comprehensive care

“I really want to honor patients’ trust in me”

Note: The terms "survivor" and "victim" are used based on personal preference and can reflect an individual's healing journey.

Areas of concern

Our research revealed four critical issues affecting trauma survivors' healthcare experiences:

Lack of Patient education

Patients feel uninformed about appointment & need more control over their appointments and rights.

Unsupportive Exam Room Environments

Exam rooms must foster trust and comfort through improved physical space and doctor-patient interactions.

Insufficient Provider Time & Preparedness

Providers need more time, confidence, and training to deliver trauma-informed care.

Fragmented Care Across Providers

A holistic view of the patient across different providers and therapists is needed to avoid re-disclosure of trauma and dissociation.

DESIGN PROCESS

Thorough, Iterative ideation

Lot's of sketches and mid-fidelity prototypes

We brainstormed, mind-mapped and sketched our ideas on how we could address the painpoints.

Some of our many ideas. Click on image to read.

USER TESTING & ITERATION

Trial & Error

We conducted usability tests with 4 people & tasked them navigate booking an appointment on our Mid Fidelity prototypes.

While some things went well, there was plenty of room for improvement.

Selecting Exams during appointment booking

Information about due examinations

Viewing patient rights

User Surveys & Interviews

Aiming for a comprehensive rounded view, we reached out far & wide to survivors, healthcare professionals, educators & organizations to collect their insights and experiences by sending out surveys.

FINAL RESULT

Three phased solution

After thorough research, my team and I pinpointed the three key phases of a patient's journey and crafted a series of interconnected solutions for each phase, that functions together as a unified, holistic approach:

01

Before Care

Booking & Checking into the Appointment

02

In the moment of Care

Physical Appointment experience

03

After Care

Effective feedback mechanisms

01 Before Care – Appointment Booking & Check-in

I scoured existing resources & communities via various reddit threads and forums like nurse.com to learn about survivors' pelvic exam experiences and trauma-informed care through healthcare professionals and patients.

Patients can view information & pre-select exams they're due for

This ensures that they know what to expect from their appointment.

Patients can choose to disclose any

history of trauma

& request special accommodations.

Patient Rights are displayed clearly before submitting the consent form

When checking into the clinic, in addition to signing forms,  patient receives another walkthrough of their rights & what to expect from their appointment.

This gives patients another opportunity to better prepare themselves while they wait.

02 In the moment of Care – Customizable environment & comfort box

Patients can control temperature levels, room lighting, choose calming ceiling projections and hospital approved aroma diffusers via tablets owned by the clinic.

This enables further

patient autonomy and personalization.

Revamping other tangible aspects like calm-colored walls and chairs positioned under a patient’s line of sight, together with a comfort box stocked with items like stress balls, warming pads, lubricant heaters etc., enhances

03 After Care – Appointment Booking & Check-in

A post-consultation review questionnaire, carefully

designed to gather impressions of a patient's visit for future reference to aid healthcare practitioners provide the best care.

This empowers patients to reflect and shape their future care.

REFLECTION & LEARNING

Looking back

Online Netnography

I scoured existing resources & communities via various reddit threads and forums like nurse.com to learn about survivors' pelvic exam experiences and trauma-informed care through healthcare professionals and patients.

Empathy in Sensitive Contexts

Working on sensitive topics like trauma requires great care, empathy, and thoughtfulness in design. It's safe to say that I've grown in my ability to consider the emotional impact of design choices and to create experiences that promote well-being.

Small Changes, Big Impact

Working on this showed that even seemingly small changes, like a few extra steps during the booking process, can have a significant impact on patient experiences and outcomes. It's a reminder that there are always opportunities to make meaningful improvements in healthcare.

Getting feedback, Making it Real

To refine our design and ensure it truly resonates, I want to seek feedback from a diverse range of survivors and providers. To drive meaningful change, I want to engage with key decision-makers who have the power to turn our speculative design into a reality within healthcare systems.

Team FourGood beaming after a successful presentation

Analysing meetings for mental well-being

How might we transform workplace interactions into opportunities for genuine emotional growth and early mental health support?

roxHealth brings "a new social contract in mental health" through an innovative platform that analyzes meeting interactions to help professionals build confidence and develop stronger communication skills.

The platform combines meeting analysis with guided journaling to provide personalized insights and development paths. Backed by Microsoft for Startups, GitHub Accelerator, and Atlassian for Startups.

During my time here I worked on end-to-end product design including user research, competitive analysis, interface design, and strategy development. I also collaborated with CEO & product lead to define product vision and execution roadmap.

Meeting Analysis

The platform analyzes multiple dimensions of communication during video meetings:

Communication pattern analysis

Personalized skill development insights

Guided reflection prompts

Progress tracking and feedback loops

This approach helps users understand their communication patterns and build confidence in professional settings.
